dataset: Monochromatic wavelength (380-780 nm, 1 nm) to display sRGB, two variants
calc: For each wavelength, XYZ = (x_bar, y_bar, z_bar) from cie1931-2deg-cmf.json (the tristimulus response to a unit-radiance monochromatic stimulus). Converted to linear sRGB with the D65 XYZ->sRGB matrix (IEC 61966-2-1 primaries; matrix values per Bruce Lindbloom's published derivation, self-checked here to send the D65 white point to (1,1,1)). Most spectral colors fall outside the sRGB gamut (at least one channel negative); gamut-mapped by blending toward the D65 white point AT CONSTANT Y (so hue angle and luminance both move continuously with wavelength, and adjacent wavelengths never collapse onto the same clipped RGB) until every channel is >= 0, then sRGB-encoded (IEC 61966-2-1 OETF). 'natural' keeps the CMF's own y_bar as the luminance, so it dims sharply toward 380 and 780 nm (matches real photopic sensitivity, but is nearly black there -- unsuitable for drawing photon sparks you want to see). 'display' first rescales XYZ so Y = 0.5 for every wavelength (a uniform scale preserves x,y chromaticity, i.e. hue and saturation, exactly) before the same constant-Y desaturation, so every wavelength renders at the same brightness -- intended for the photon-rain / ray-fan visualizations, where wavelength should read as color, and photon count/exposure should read as brightness, per the brief's 'what you see is computed' + 'clarity beats glow' rules. desaturation_t records how far each wavelength had to move toward white (0 = already in gamut, 1 = fully desaturated to white); high values flag wavelengths the sRGB gamut represents poorly (mainly 380-430 nm and 520-560 nm).
unit: linear: 0-1 linear-light sRGB; encoded: 0-1 gamma-encoded sRGB (IEC 61966-2-1 OETF)
gamut_mapping: desaturate toward CIE D65 white point at constant Y (see calc)
